[2023 summer phd probability — problem 4]

Part I, Problem. Let $(X_i)_{i\ge1}$ be i.i.d. with $P(X_i > 0) = 1$, $\mathbb{E}[\sqrt{X_i}] < \infty$ but $\mathbb{E}[X_i] = +\infty$; write $\mu = \mathbb{E}[\sqrt{X_i}]$. You may use that $\int_1^{+\infty} u^{-\alpha}\,du < \infty$ for $\alpha > 1$ and $\lim_n (1 - c/n)^n = e^{-c}$.
(1) Applying the LLN to $\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n \sqrt{X_i}$, prove $P(\sum_{i=1}^n X_i \le (\mu + \varepsilon)^2 n^2) \to 1$ for any constant $\varepsilon > 0$.
(2) For fixed $s \in (\tfrac12, 1]$ and i.i.d. $(X_i)$ with $P(X_i > u) = u^{-s}$ for $u \ge 1$, find the range and density of $X_i$. (Use this density for parts 3-5.)
(3) Prove $\mathbb{E}[\sqrt{X_i}] < \infty$.
(4) For real $y > 1$, express $P(\max_{i\le n} X_i > y)$ as a function of $P(X_1 > y)$ and $n$ only.
(5) Find $\lim_{n\to\infty} P(\max_{i\le n} X_i > n^{1/s})$.
(6) Is it possible, for any i.i.d. $(X_i)$ with $\mathbb{E}[\sqrt{X_i}] < \infty$, that $\lim_n P(\sum_{i=1}^n X_i \le C n^{1.99}) = 1$ for a constant $C > 0$?

response.text:
Let  
\[
S_n=\sum_{i=1}^n X_i,\qquad M_n=\max_{1\le i\le n}X_i.
\]

## (1)

Set \(Y_i=\sqrt{X_i}\). Since \(\mathbb E[\sqrt{X_i}]<\infty\), the \(Y_i\) are integrable i.i.d. random variables with mean \(\mu\). By the Strong Law of Large Numbers,

\[
\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n \sqrt{X_i}\to \mu \qquad \text{a.s.}
\]

In particular,

\[
P\left(\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n \sqrt{X_i}\le \mu+\varepsilon\right)\to 1.
\]

Now, since \(X_i>0\),

\[
\sum_{i=1}^n X_i=\sum_{i=1}^n (\sqrt{X_i})^2
\le \left(\sum_{i=1}^n \sqrt{X_i}\right)^2,
\]

because the square on the right contains additional nonnegative cross terms. Therefore, on the event

\[
\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n \sqrt{X_i}\le \mu+\varepsilon,
\]

we have

\[
\sum_{i=1}^n X_i
\le \left(n(\mu+\varepsilon)\right)^2
=(\mu+\varepsilon)^2n^2.
\]

Thus

\[
P\left(S_n\le (\mu+\varepsilon)^2n^2\right)
\ge 
P\left(\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n \sqrt{X_i}\le \mu+\varepsilon\right)\to 1.
\]

Hence

\[
\boxed{
P\left(\sum_{i=1}^n X_i\le (\mu+\varepsilon)^2n^2\right)\to 1.
}
\]

---

## (2)

We are given, for \(u\ge 1\),

\[
P(X_i>u)=u^{-s},\qquad s\in \left(\frac12,1\right].
\]

At \(u=1\),

\[
P(X_i>1)=1,
\]

so \(X_i>1\) almost surely. Therefore the range is \((1,\infty)\) almost surely.

For \(x>1\), the CDF is

\[
F(x)=P(X_i\le x)=1-P(X_i>x)=1-x^{-s}.
\]

For \(x\le 1\),

\[
F(x)=0.
\]

Thus

\[
F(x)=
\begin{cases}
0, & x\le 1,\\
1-x^{-s}, & x>1.
\end{cases}
\]

Differentiating for \(x>1\), the density is

\[
f(x)=s x^{-s-1},\qquad x>1.
\]

So

\[
\boxed{
f(x)=s x^{-s-1}\mathbf 1_{\{x>1\}}.
}
\]

---

## (3)

Using the density from part (2),

\[
\mathbb E[\sqrt{X_i}]
=
\int_1^\infty \sqrt{x}\,s x^{-s-1}\,dx.
\]

Thus

\[
\mathbb E[\sqrt{X_i}]
=
s\int_1^\infty x^{1/2}x^{-s-1}\,dx
=
s\int_1^\infty x^{-s-1/2}\,dx.
\]

The integral converges exactly when

\[
s+\frac12>1,
\]

i.e.

\[
s>\frac12.
\]

Since \(s\in(1/2,1]\), the expectation is finite. In fact,

\[
\mathbb E[\sqrt{X_i}]
=
s\int_1^\infty x^{-s-1/2}\,dx
=
\frac{s}{s-\frac12}<\infty.
\]

Therefore

\[
\boxed{\mathbb E[\sqrt{X_i}]<\infty.}
\]

---

## (4)

Let \(y>1\). By independence,

\[
P(M_n\le y)
=
P(X_1\le y,\dots,X_n\le y)
=
P(X_1\le y)^n.
\]

Therefore

\[
P(M_n>y)
=
1-P(M_n\le y)
=
1-P(X_1\le y)^n.
\]

Since

\[
P(X_1\le y)=1-P(X_1>y),
\]

we get

\[
\boxed{
P(M_n>y)=1-\left(1-P(X_1>y)\right)^n.
}
\]

For this particular distribution, \(P(X_1>y)=y^{-s}\), so

\[
\boxed{
P(M_n>y)=1-(1-y^{-s})^n.
}
\]

---

## (5)

Take \(y=n^{1/s}\). Then

\[
P(X_1>n^{1/s})
=
(n^{1/s})^{-s}
=
n^{-1}.
\]

Using part (4),

\[
P(M_n>n^{1/s})
=
1-\left(1-\frac1n\right)^n.
\]

By the given limit,

\[
\left(1-\frac1n\right)^n\to e^{-1}.
\]

Therefore

\[
\boxed{
\lim_{n\to\infty}P(M_n>n^{1/s})=1-e^{-1}.
}
\]

---

## (6)

No. In general, one cannot replace the exponent \(2\) in part (1) by \(1.99\).

Choose

\[
s\in\left(\frac12,\frac{1}{1.99}\right).
\]

This is possible because

\[
\frac{1}{1.99}=\frac{100}{199}> \frac12.
\]

Let \(X_i\) have tail

\[
P(X_i>u)=u^{-s},\qquad u\ge 1.
\]

By part (3),

\[
\mathbb E[\sqrt{X_i}]<\infty.
\]

But now

\[
\frac1s>1.99.
\]

Fix any constant \(C>0\). Since

\[
\frac{n^{1/s}}{C n^{1.99}}
=
\frac{1}{C}n^{1/s-1.99}\to \infty,
\]

we have, for all sufficiently large \(n\),

\[
n^{1/s}>C n^{1.99}.
\]

Therefore, for large \(n\),

\[
\{M_n>n^{1/s}\}\subseteq \{S_n>Cn^{1.99}\}.
\]

Hence

\[
P(S_n\le Cn^{1.99})
\le
P(M_n\le n^{1/s}).
\]

By part (5),

\[
P(M_n>n^{1/s})\to 1-e^{-1},
\]

so

\[
P(M_n\le n^{1/s})\to e^{-1}.
\]

Thus

\[
\limsup_{n\to\infty}P(S_n\le Cn^{1.99})
\le e^{-1}<1.
\]

Therefore the probability cannot converge to \(1\). Hence

\[
\boxed{
\text{No, such a bound with exponent }1.99\text{ does not hold in general.}
}
\]
